title: Why Your Achilles tendon Matter More Than Muscle (The Achilles training Episode)
description: The strongest tendon in your body is a spring, and it does more for your jump than your calf muscle ever will. The heel drop test grades that spring one slow rep at a time. Get your number, learn why skinny legs bounce better, and start training the cable that launches you.

scenes.narration: Stand on the edge of a step with the ball of one foot on it and your heel hanging off the back. Use both feet to rise up onto your toes, then lift the other foot away and lower yourself down on the one leg, taking a full three seconds to sink until your heel drops below the step. That slow drop is one rep. Count how many perfect three second drops you can do before your calf shakes, your heel starts falling fast, or you need the wall for more than balance. Do both legs and write down the lower number. This is the exact movement clinics use to rebuild the strongest tendon in your body, and today it is your test. Keep your number. At the end I will tell you what it says about your spring.

beats.text: BALL OF FOOT ON THE STEP
RISE WITH TWO, DROP WITH ONE

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN SOFT AND WIRED
scenes.sub: under 8: soft spring - over 20: kangaroo cable
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Fifteen slow heel drops on your weaker leg is where a soft spring becomes a wired one. Under eight, your Achilles is untrained, and untrained here explains more flat jumps and tired calves than any muscle weakness. Eight to fifteen means the spring works but leaks energy on the way down, which is the difference between landing quietly and landing heavily. Over twenty, you own a spring that returns force like it was built for sport, because that is literally its job. This test never asks how big your calves look. It asks how the cable behaves under a slow, honest load, and behavior is what jumping is made of.

Look at the back of your ankle. The Achilles is the thickest, strongest tendon in your entire body, connecting both of your calf muscles to your heel bone. Its job is not really to pull. Its job is to store and return. When your foot lands, the tendon stretches under loads of several times your bodyweight, banking the energy like a drawn bow. When you push off, it pays the energy back, and a large share of your running and jumping power comes from this refund rather than from fresh muscle work. Your calf muscle is honestly the junior partner here. It tensions the spring and fine tunes it, but the spring does the spectacular part. That is why this channel trains the cable, not just the muscle on top of it.

beats.text: THE MUSCLE IS THE JUNIOR PARTNER

scenes.narration: Here is the comparison that changes how you train legs. A bigger calf mostly gives you a bigger engine for tensioning the spring, but a stiffer, better trained spring gives you more free energy on every single step and jump. Sprinters and jumpers do not win because of giant calves. Plenty of them are built like you. They win because their Achilles returns energy so efficiently that the ground barely gets to keep any. When researchers slow down elite jumpers, the muscle work looks surprisingly ordinary and the tendon work looks extraordinary. Your heel drop number is the home version of that lab test. It grades how much of a spring you are currently walking around on.

Now the mistake that keeps Achilles tendons weak and grumpy. People train calves with fast, bouncy, half range reps, chasing a burn, and the tendon learns almost nothing because the load is chaotic. Worse, they jump straight into sprinting or box jumps on a spring that has never been loaded slowly, and the tendon complains loudly. The order matters. Slow heavy drops first, teaching the cable to organize load. Isometric holds in the middle position when it is irritable. Speed work last, once the spring has earned it. Every clinic on earth rebuilds this tendon in that order, and athletes come back from ruptures following it. Your training should steal the same order before you ever need the clinic version.

Here is your free daily audit, and it happens before your feet find the floor. The first steps out of bed tell the truth about this tendon. A spring that is adapting well feels quiet in the morning. A spring that is overloaded reports stiffness in the first ten steps, because tendon tissue thickens slightly overnight and an irritated one announces itself before it warms up. Coaches who manage jumpers for a living literally score the season by those morning steps. You can steal the system: rate your first steps from one to ten each morning while you train this. If the number trends better, the dose is right. If it trends worse two days running, the dose was too big, no matter what the plan said. The tendon keeps honest books. Learn to read them and you will never need to guess about your training again.

Time for the skinny advantage, and at the Achilles it might be the biggest one on this channel. A spring returns energy best when it is not overloaded, and your light frame loads the Achilles with far less bodyweight on every landing. The heavy guy's spring spends its budget just surviving his mass. Yours has budget left over to return, which is why light athletes bounce and heavy ones thud. You also get to train this tendon almost daily, because the dose per session is self limiting and recovery is fast at your weight. Same tendon, same test, completely different economics. Your build is not a jumping disadvantage. It is a spring waiting for training.
Train with me. Four rounds of heel drops, forty seconds per leg, twenty seconds of rest between rounds. Rise with two feet, drop with one, three full seconds down. Go.

Here is your week. Heel drops once a day, two sets per leg, always at the three second tempo, on a step when you have one. Add a forty five second mid position hold on restless days, heel hovering at step level, to keep the tendon fed between sessions. Progress by slowing down before you add anything: four second drops beat a backpack every time at this stage. Expect the tendon to feel worked the next morning and plan around that, because this tissue reports a day late. And the warning that protects your spring. Achilles pain that is sharp, swollen, or still there after two weeks of sensible loading — see a professional if it persists, and get it checked before you train through it.

beats.title: THIS TISSUE REPORTS A DAY LATE

scenes.label: THE RETEST LINE IN 30 DAYS
scenes.sub: under 8: untrained - 8 to 15: building - over 15: wired
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under eight: your spring is untrained, and the daily drops will start stiffening it within weeks. Eight to fifteen: you are building, and the four second tempo is your next level. Over fifteen: your Achilles is wired, and speed work has officially been earned. Put your number in the comments, weaker leg, just the number. We retest in thirty days with the same step and the same three second rule. Springs do not lie, and neither will the retest.

The strongest tendon in your body is a spring, and today you found out how much bounce is actually in it. Drop slowly every day, and in thirty days we measure the spring again. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
